A 63-year-old woman presented to our department with a 6-month history of recurrent vomiting and loss of 5 kg in weight. The patient had a medical history of dyslipidaemia and hypertension; she was prescribed rosuvastatin and olmesartan. She had no history of gastrointestinal disorders, recent foreign travel, or infection with Helicobacter pylori.
On examination, she was generally unwell and underweight; her blood pressure was 150/88 mm Hg, pulse was 70 beats per min, oxygen saturation was 99%, and BMI was 16 kg/m2. We found no lymphadenopathy, and abdominal examination found no masses or ascites.
Laboratory investigations showed normal complete blood count—including a typical eosinophil count; carcinoembryonic antigen, soluble interleukin-2 receptor, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody tests were within normal range. Antinuclear antibody titre was 1:160 (normal value <1:40) and serum immunoglobulin E was 700 IU/mL (typical range 0–100).
An oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD) showed a distended stomach with linear scars and a rough atrophic mucosa that bled easily upon contact (figure). Histopathological examination of a sample obtained by gastric biopsy showed subepithelial collagen deposition with inflammatory cell infiltration—including eosinophils (figure); the small and large intestines showed no specific findings.
At this stage, our working diagnosis included collagenous gastritis, eosinophilic gastritis, and autoimmune gastritis. And based on these working diagnoses, the patient was prescribed a proton pump inhibitor—esomeprazole 20 mg orally—which did not result in any improvement.
Further review of the medical history found that the patient had been taking olmesartan 20 mg daily for the past decade and we considered that it may have been responsible for the patient's symptoms; we therefore decided to stop it.
2 weeks later, the patient stopped vomiting and within 2 months she had gained 7 kg. A repeat OGD, 6 months post-discontinuation, showed a substantial improvement in mucosal inflammation; histopathological examination of samples obtained by biopsies, showed no evidence of residual collagen bands or significant inflammatory cell infiltration (appendix). And at 2 years after discontinuation of the olmesartan no recurrence was seen. Regarding the patient's hypertension, azelnidipine 8 mg daily was prescribed as an alternative treatment.
Collagenous gastritis is characterised by patchy subepithelial collagen bands and inflammatory cell infiltration, including eosinophils; such features can appear in other types of gastritis with similar inflammatory cell infiltration—including eosinophilic gastritis, coeliac disease, and autoimmune gastritis—necessitating a high index of suspicion to make an accurate pathological diagnosis. The precise pathogenesis of collagenous gastritis remains poorly understood and no available treatments are established owing to its rarity; associations with certain medications—including olmesartan as in our patient—have been suggested.

A 35-year-old woman complaining of weakness of her left arm and leg was admitted to our hospital. She said the problem started 25 h earlier, soon after liposuction on her left thigh and a filler injection of the fat into her face in a beauty salon. The woman was previously healthy with no medical history. On physical examination we found hemiplegia of the left limbs: muscle strength was 1/5 in the arm and 3/5 in the leg. She had left central facial palsy and clear speech, and was cognitively intact. Bilateral Babinski signs were negative and there were no features of meningeal irritation. The patient's blood pressure, pulse rate, and temperature were in the normal ranges. Routine blood tests, blood lipids, glucose concentration, and electrolytes were also normal. An electrocardiogram and a transthoracic echocardiogram showed no abnormalities.A CT scan of the woman's brain showed a low-density strip (appendix) in the right middle cerebral artery (MCA) that was hyperintense on T1, T2, and T2 fluid-attenuated inversion recovery weighted MRIs (figure; appendix). Additionally, the MRI showed an area of infarction in the region supplied by the right MCA. Magnetic resonance angiography (appendix) showed an occlusion of part of the right MCA and a low-density filling defect in the initial segment of the right external carotid artery—which, on an ultrasound scan, was hyperechoic—indicative of an embolus (figure).
Considering all the information in the round, we decided that the patient had a cerebral fat embolism (CFE) following the injection into her face of autologous fat. We decided to treat her conservatively with oral aspirin 0·2 g once daily, oral atorvastatin 40 mg once daily, and intravenous dexamethasone 10 mg once daily. After 1 week, the patient's symptoms began to resolve and after 2 weeks she was transferred to the rehabilitation department. 3 months after she came into hospital, she was able to walk unaided.
A stroke in a young person can be caused by emboli, atherosclerotic disease, vasculopathies, or subarachnoid or intraparenchymal bleeding. Other causes particularly important in the younger age group are oral contraceptive use, pregnancy and postpartum states, substance use, trauma, and migraine. CFE—a thankfully rarely reported complication of cosmetic procedures—more usually occurs after fractures of the long bones.
How the fat from an autologous facial filler reaches the arterial network is unclear. It may be that during the injection the needle penetrates a small artery. Then, possibly due to continuous pressure applied during the injection, the fat travels, against the normal blood flow, up the small artery, through the facial artery and the external carotid artery, into the internal carotid artery.
CFE is usually self-limiting. The key with a presentation of rapid onset of left-sided weakness—such as in our patient—is to make the right diagnosis as soon as possible.

input: A 41-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of progressive vision loss and headaches. MRI revealed a large sellar tumour with suprasellar extension, which was deemed a probable pituitary macroadenoma (figure A, B). The patient underwent transsphenoidal surgery because of visual field defects and headaches. Histological analysis after surgery revealed a giant cell tumour of bone (GCTB) and symptoms improved; however, 2 months later the large sellar–clival remnant compressing the optic chiasm (figure C, D) motivated a second surgery by pterional craniotomy. After surgery, tumour regrowth occurred (figure E, F), causing diplopia and blurred vision. A third decompressing operation aiming for maximal debulking before denosumab commencement was done endoscopically; however, only partial tumour removal was achieved (figure G, H). Denosumab (120 mg subcutaneously every 28 days) was initiated, and a marked response was noted after 6 months of treatment (figure I, J). After 14 months of denosumab, the patient remained symptom-free without needing further operations (figure K, L).GCTB represent 5–10% of bone tumours, classically affect long bones (<1% of all GCTB have a cranial location) and, although benign, can be locally aggressive. GCTB are histologically characterised by large multinucleated giant cells, but the clinical or radiological differential diagnosis can be challenging. Denosumab, an inhibitor of receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand (RANKL), can be used to treat GCTB, because RANKL is overexpressed by mononuclear neoplastic stromal cells. As shown here, denosumab should also be considered in the early management of sellar–clival GCTB. This case also highlights the sustained reduction in tumour mass achieved by denosumab, sparing the patient from further operations. If feasible, surgical resection is still preferable as the definitive treatment, because the effect of denosumab wears off after stopping treatment and tumour regrowth can occur. Lifelong denosumab treatment will thus be likely required in this case; however, increasing the intervals between denosumab administration can be attempted to prevent or minimise adverse events, such as osteonecrosis of the jaw or atypical femoral fractures. Although GCTB is usually managed by rheumatologists, oncologists, or orthopaedics, sellar or parasellar GCTB might be first seen by endocrinologists, ophthalmologists, or neurosurgeons, who should be aware of this entity and the potential role of denosumab in its management.
output: Giant Cell Tumour of Bone (GCTB) of the sellar-clival region

A 20-year-old woman presented with a history of right-sided headaches associated with rapid worsening of vision in the right eye over a period of a few days. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity of finger counting close to the face and a relative afferent pupillary defect was found in the right eye. Fundus examination of the right eye revealed retinal vasculitis with extensive perivascular sheathing resembling a so-called frosted branch appearance with disc oedema and haemorrhages (figure A, video). There were haemorrhages in the posterior pole with vascular sheathing (vasculitis) along the inferiotemporal vascular arcade (figure B). Fundus fluorescence angiography of the right eye revealed disc leakage with perivascular leakage and blocked fluorescence at the macula (figure C). Optical coherence tomography revealed macular oedema. The left eye was healthy. Blood tests revealed anaemia, lymphopenia with an absolute CD4 count of 149 cells per mm3 (normal range: 500–1500 cells per mm3), reduced glomerular filtration rate, blood urea concentration of 131 mg/dL, serum creatinine concentration of 4·9 mg/dL, and microscopic haematuria with occasional red blood cell casts. 24-h urinary protein concentration was 2·8 g. Blood serology for viruses, including HIV, was negative. Vitreous fluid testing for cytomegalovirus DNA was negative. Blood autoantibody panel showed myeloperoxidase antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) ELISA positivity with 101 U/mL (normal range: <5 U/mL). A kidney biopsy was completed for histopathological investigation and hematoxylin and eosin staining used, which revealed necrotising crescentic nephritis (figure D) and many fibrotic crescents along with interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy, no different test or stain was used, these pathological features were not visible in the image. Immunofluorescence revealed an absence of immune complexes (figure E). A diagnosis of microscopic polyangiitis with frosted branch angiitis of the retina and pauci-immune necrotising crescentic glomerulonephritis was made. The patient was treated with corticosteroids (three intravenous pulses of methylprednisone followed by oral prednisone with a starting dose of 1 mg/kg per day) and oral cyclophosphamide (2 mg/kg per day in 2 divided doses), which resulted in a gradual improvement of vision in the affected right eye. After 3 months of treatment, at the last outpatient visit, her creatinine concentration had decreased to 2·4 mg/dL, she had a blood urea concentration of 65 mg/dL, and her haemoglobin and CD4 counts improved. At 3 months post-disgnosis proteinuria had decreased to 1·1 g/24 h. Visual acuity in the right eye had improved to 6/36. Fundus examination showed marked resolution of retinal vasculitis with a few haemorrhages.
The term frosted branch angiitis encompasses a rare, vision-threatening, non-occlusive retinal perivasculitis with perivascular exudate causing severe retinal vessel sheathing resembling frosted tree branches. Retinal frosted branch angiitis is classified into three categories: type 1, associated with malignancy (leukaemia or lymphoma); type 2, associated with viral or bacterial infections, or autoimmune conditions; and type 3, primary idiopathic. Rheumatological disorders associated with retinal frosted branch angiitis include granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, systemic lupus erythematosus, antiphospholipid syndrome, sarcoidosis, and Behçet's disease. In ANCA-associated vasculitis, lymphopenia with a low disease-related CD4 count is not uncommon, and is due to increased activation of CD4 T cells and their redistribution to the vessels and tissues. A low CD4 count has also been shown to be a risk factor for developing retinal vasculitis. Retinal vasculitis in ANCA-associated vasculitis is a rare occurrence and is an occlusive vasculopathy resulting from fibrinoid necrosis and secondary thrombosis. However, a few cases of frosted branch angiitis have been reported with granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis. The hypothesis for frosted branch angiitis in ANCA-associated vasculitis is that it represents an extreme form of a diffuse perivasculitis with movement of inflammatory cells in large numbers from the vascular wall into the retina causing sheathing due to inflammation-induced disruption of the blood retinal barrier. In this patient, the relative compartmentalisation of CD4 lymphocytes in the retinal vasculature could have caused the peripheral lymphopenia.
The outcome of primary idiopathic frosted branch angiitis is favourable with a good response to corticosteroids. The outcome of secondary frosted branch angiitis (ie, type 1 and 2), including that in ANCA-associated vasculitis, is variable and is negatively influenced by the severity of the underlying disorder and the delay in diagnosis.

A 76-year-old man who had a 2-day history being unwell—starting with sweating and a fever that then developed into delirium—was admitted to the emergency room of a local general hospital; he then had a generalised tonic-clonic seizure without recovering consciousness. The patient was transferred to our intensive care unit after orotracheal intubation and initiation of invasive mechanical ventilation.
1 month earlier, the patient had radiofrequency catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation refractory to both medication and electrical cardioversion. The patient had a medical history of atrial fibrillation, hypertension, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease; he was prescribed apixaban, bisoprolol, dapagliflozin, furosemide, and metformin.
On examination, the patient was in a coma—Glasgow Coma Score 6; pupils were reactive and symmetrical. He had no sensory or motor deficits or focal neurological signs. Blood pressure was 113/52 mm Hg, heart rate 83 beats per min, oxygen saturation was in typical range, and temperature was 39·6°C.
Laboratory investigations found a biological inflammatory syndrome (C-reactive protein concentration was 177 mg/L [typical range <10]; white blood cell count was 15 000 per mm [typical range 4000–10 000]; and troponin was 3309 ng/L [typical range <5]).
A CT scan of the patient's brain showed diffuse pneumocephalus (figure); brain ischaemia was confirmed by hyperintense signals on MRI FLAIR T2-weighted sequences (figure).
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy was immediately started which effectively dissolved the cerebral air embolism (appendix); the patient had two sessions, 24 h apart, in our hyperbaric chamber receiving invasive mechanical ventilation—3 atmospheres of pressure with the fraction of inspired oxygen at 100% for 2 h.
We suspected the cerebral air embolism had come from an atrio-oesophageal fistula by a process of elimination: none of the common sources of pneumocephalus—including an intravenous line, or a recent endoscopy or laparoscopy—were identified in our patient. The absence of any abnormalities on clinical examination and the recent history of catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation further added to our conviction of an atrio-oesophageal fistula.
A chest CT angiogram showed a filiform hypodense signal within the left atrium anterior to the opening of the right inferior pulmonary vein and extending to the posterior wall of the left atrium communicating with the oesophagus, suggestive of an atrio-oesophageal fistula (figure). Delayed phase contrast-enhanced CT scanning showed recurrence of an air bubble in the left atrium—confirming air leakage (figure).
The patient had surgery to close the fistula with oesophagostomy immediately on completion of the hyperbaric oxygen therapy and more than 24 h after the onset of symptoms. However, due to the presence of diffuse brain ischaemia seen on MRI done prior to the hyperbaric oxygen therapy and following discussion with the patient's relatives, active treatment was withdrawn. The patient died 1 week after admission to the intensive care unit.
Atrio-oesophageal fistula complicating catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation can—as in our patient—result in air embolism. Cerebral air embolism can result in acute ischaemia and cerebral oedema that may mimic the presentation of other stroke syndromes; prompt hyperbaric oxygen therapy is the mainstay of treatment.
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy decreases the size of bubbles because of an increase in ambient pressure and a rapid lowering of nitrogen levels that optimises oxygenation of poorly perfused brain tissue; it remains the gold standard treatment for cerebral air embolism with excellent results when initiated immediately.

output: Cerebral air embolism secondary to iatrogenic atrio-oesophageal fistula following radiofrequency catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation
target: Atrio-oesophageal fistula complicating atrial fibrillation radiofrequency ablation

A 61-year-old who was receiving long-term treatment with prednisone for refractory idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura required a dose increase after a large decrease in platelet count (6×109/L). He had had his spleen removed 7 years earlier. He was not on any other medication and there was no evidence of pseudothrombocytopenia, lymphoprolipherative disease, malignancies, or Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. Serological tests were negative for HIV, Epstein Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, antinuclear antibodies, and lupus anticoagulant. Stool specimen was negative for Helicobacter pylori. 24 h later he developed pigmented vesicles on the left side of his trunk, left arm, and left hand. Segmental distribution of the painful cutaneous lesions suggested haemorrhagic herpes zoster. Prednisone was stopped and the patient was treated with intravenous immunoglobulin G (1 g/kg daily for 4 days) and valacyclovir (1 g three times daily). He had a rapid increase in platelet count and uneventful recovery. Haemorrhagic herpes zoster is an atypical form of cutaneous varicella zoster virus and correlates with immunodepression, coagulopathy, or thrombocytopenia.

A 60-year-old Japanese man was referred to our hospital because of an abnormal endoscopic finding in the oesophagus at a regular health check. He reported receiving no medication and had no history of alcohol misuse. The patient was a former smoker and reported sometimes feeling heartburn. Laboratory data revealed no pronounced abnormalities. An esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed short segment Barrett's oesophagus and a whitish elevated lesion adjacent to the Barrett's oesophagus lesion (figure, A). Vessel structures could not be seen by magnified narrow band imaging, because of a whitish plaque (figure, B). Chromoendoscopy with Lugol's iodine solution showed decreased staining of the lesion (figure, C). A biopsy was done, and histology confirmed cell proliferation of the squamous epithelium. Although cellular atypicality was mild, we considered the lesion to be potentially malignant. Therefore, an endoscopic submucosal dissection was done for an en-bloc complete resection and diagnosis. Histology showed papillary growth and nests of well differentiated squamous epithelium pushing into the underlying stroma, which is typical of oesophageal verrucous carcinoma (figure, D). Pathological examination revealed tumour depth invasion into the lamina propria mucosa (stage T1a) without lymphovascular invasion. The patient was monitored closely and no recurrence had occurred at 3 months after the endoscopic submucosal dissection.Oesophageal verrucous carcinoma is a very rare malignancy. Although, the cause of such lesions is debated, it has been suggested that oesophageal verrucous carcinoma is associated with achalasia, acid reflux, and alcohol and nicotine misuse. The common endoscopic appearance of most oesophageal verrucous carcinomas is an elevated whitish plaque that is clearly circumscribed. Oesophageal verrucous carcinomas are difficult to diagnose before surgical resection. Accurate diagnosis is often delayed because the endoscopic finding of a whitish plaque is similar to a Candida infection and squamous cell papilloma. In addition, superficial biopsies are frequently false negative for malignancy because of highly differentiated histology. Endoscopic resection can be curative for oesophageal verrucous carcinoma restricted to the epithelium and the lamina propria mucosa. A lack of recognition of oesophageal verrucous carcinoma leads to a delay in diagnosis and progression of the disease. To improve the chance of curative treatment, endoscopists need to recognise the macroscopic findings and frequent difficulties associated with diagnosis of oesophageal verrucous carcinoma.

A 29-year-old man presented to the outpatient clinic with 2 months of bright red blood from the rectum. He had no fever, weight loss, diarrhea, or hematuria. He lived in the interior of northeastern Brazil and regularly bathed in rivers. On physical examination, he had slight tenderness to palpation of the left flank. Laboratory testing was notable for an absolute eosinophil count of 470 per cubic millimeter (reference range, 34 to 420). A colonoscopy identified a reddish, polypoid lesion in the distal rectum. Biopsy of the lesion revealed a dense inflammatory infiltrate containing eosinophils and schistosome eggs. What is the appropriate treatment for this condition?
output: Schistosoma mansoni infection with rectal schistosomal polyp

input: A 30-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of progressive skin lesions on her face. On physical examination, there were hyperpigmented, yellow, papillomatous papules and plaques on the face (left). Hyperpigmented velvety plaques were also seen on the skin of the neck, groin and axillae. She also reported new-onset heartburn, fatigue, and unintentional 15-kg weight loss. A skin biopsy of the facial lesion showed epidermal papillomatosis, acanthosis, hyperkeratosis, and negative staining for human papillomavirus. A computed tomography (CT) of the  abdomen and pelvis was performed (right). What is the most likely diagnosis?
output: Glucagonoma syndrome due to pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor
